notes.title: Key facts by topic
notes.html:
Functions & transformations

  • Input and output — A function is a rule that turns every input into exactly one output, like a vending machine: press B4 and you always get the same snack.
  • Function notation — f(x) is read “f of x”. It means: use the rule f on the number x. To find f(4), put 4 into the rule.
  • Tables, graphs and the vertical line test — A graph shows a function if no vertical line touches it twice. If one input had two outputs, the machine would be broken.

Quadratics & complex numbers

  • Squares and square roots — A square with side s has area s². Going backwards, √(s²) = s. Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.
  • Solving by factoring — If two numbers multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. So (x − p)(x − q) = 0 means x = p or x = q.
  • Vertex form — y = a(x − h)² + k has its turning point at (h, k). It opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0.

Polynomials

  • Powers and terms — x³ means x · x · x. A term is a number times powers of x. A polynomial is a sum of terms. Its degree is the highest power.
  • Adding and multiplying polynomials — Combine like terms to add. To multiply, give every term in the first factor a turn with every term in the second.
  • Evaluating and the remainder theorem — When you divide f(x) by (x − a), the remainder is f(a). So plugging in a number is a shortcut for division.

Rational functions

  • Fractions are division — A fraction a/b means a ÷ b. You can simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the same number, like 12/18 = 2/3.
  • Rational expressions — A rational expression is a polynomial divided by a polynomial. Simplify by factoring and cancelling common factors, never by cancelling terms that are added.
  • Values that are not allowed — The denominator can never be 0. Every x that makes it 0 is left out of the domain.

Exponential functions

  • Repeated multiplication — 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. The small raised number counts how many times the base is used.
  • Doubling and tripling — If a plant doubles every day, after n days it is 2ⁿ times bigger. This kind of growth starts slowly and then explodes.
  • Exponential functions — y = a·bˣ. a is the starting amount and b is the growth factor. If b > 1 it grows. If 0 < b < 1 it decays.

Logarithms

  • What a logarithm asks — log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.
  • Common logs — log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
  • Special values — log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.

Sequences & series

  • Patterns and sequences — A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.
  • Arithmetic sequences — You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
  • Geometric sequences — You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.

Right triangles & the unit circle

  • Turns and degrees — A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
  • The sides of a right triangle — In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
  • Sine, cosine and tangent — SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.

Graphs of trig functions

  • Waves in everyday life — Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
  • The sine graph — y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.
  • Amplitude — The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.

Identities & trig equations

  • Same value, different look — An identity is an equation that is true for every allowed angle, like a rule of arithmetic that always works.
  • The Pythagorean identity — On the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Knowing one of them gives you the other.
  • Tangent from sine and cosine — tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. That is why tangent has an asymptote wherever cosine is 0.

Inverse trig functions

  • Undoing a function — An inverse function undoes another: if f turns x into y, then f⁻¹ turns y back into x. Check: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Note f⁻¹(x) is NOT 1/f(x).
  • Trig takes an angle, inverse takes a ratio — sin, cos and tan turn an angle into a ratio. sin⁻¹ (also written arcsin), cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ turn a ratio back into an angle. That is how you find a missing angle in a right triangle.
  • Why we restrict the range — Sine repeats forever, so many angles share one ratio. To make an inverse, we keep one piece: arcsin gives −90° to 90°, arccos gives 0° to 180°, arctan gives −90° to 90° (open).

Angle identities

  • Sum and difference — sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B. cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B. Notice the sign flips for cosine.
  • Double angles — Put B = A in the sum formulas: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A and cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 1 − 2 sin²A = 2 cos²A − 1.
  • Half angles — Solve the cosine double-angle formula for the half angle: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2. Pick the sign from the quadrant.

Laws of sines & cosines, vectors

  • Triangles that are not right — Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
  • Law of Sines — a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.
  • Law of Cosines — c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.

Conic sections

  • Distance and midpoint — The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.
  • Circles — A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
  • Parabolas — A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).

Polar & parametric

  • Two ways to name a point — Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.
  • Converting polar to rectangular — x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
  • Converting rectangular to polar — r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).

Limits & continuity

  • Getting closer and closer — Look at 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … The numbers never reach 1 but get as close as you like. We say they approach 1.
  • What a limit means — lim f(x) = L as x → a means f(x) gets as close to L as you want when x is close enough to a. The value at a itself does not matter.
  • Direct substitution — For polynomials and most everyday functions, just plug the number in.

Derivatives

  • Rate of change — Speed is how fast distance changes. The derivative is a rate of change at one instant, like a speedometer reading.
  • Slope of a curve — The derivative f′(x) is the slope of the tangent line at x. It is the limit of the slope between two points as they come together.
  • Power rule — d/dx of xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹. Constants disappear and constants multiplying stay.

Using derivatives

  • Position, velocity, acceleration — If s(t) is position, velocity is s′(t) and acceleration is s″(t).
  • Increasing and decreasing — If f′ > 0 the function rises. If f′ < 0 it falls. Where f′ = 0 there may be a peak or valley.
  • Critical points — Solve f′(x) = 0 to find candidates for maximum and minimum points.

Integrals

  • Area by counting — Area is how much space is inside a shape. We can estimate the area under a curve by adding up thin rectangles.
  • Riemann sums — Split the interval into slices, make a rectangle for each, and add the areas. More slices give a better estimate.
  • The definite integral — ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the exact signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Area below the axis counts as negative.

cards: A rule that gives each input exactly one output.
A function that undoes another: swaps inputs and outputs.
b² − 4ac; tells how many real roots a quadratic has.
A sum of terms that are numbers times whole-number powers of x.
An input where the function equals 0.
Dividing f(x) by (x − a) leaves remainder f(a).
(x − a) is a factor of f exactly when f(a) = 0.
written: Explain why dividing by zero is not allowed.
If a ÷ 0 = b, then b × 0 = a. But anything times 0 is 0, so no number b works unless a is 0, and then every b works. The answer is either impossible or not unique.
Why does a polynomial of degree n have at most n roots?
Each root gives a linear factor (x − r). Degree n allows at most n such factors.
bench: Rate of change on a ramp
Roll a toy car down a ramp and time it over several distances. Plot distance against time and compare the slopes.

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 10 and 14 and the angle opposite the side of length 10 is 30°. How many different triangles are possible?
sol: The height from the other vertex is h = 14 sin 30° = 7.
10 is longer than 7 but shorter than 14, so two triangles fit (the ambiguous case).

fn: A function is a rule that turns every input into exactly one output, like a vending machine: press B4 and you always get the same snack.
f(x) is read “f of x”. It means: use the rule f on the number x. To find f(4), put 4 into the rule.
Tables, graphs and the vertical line test
A graph shows a function if no vertical line touches it twice. If one input had two outputs, the machine would be broken.
The domain is every input that is allowed. The range is every output you can get. You cannot divide by zero, and you cannot take the square root of a negative number in the real numbers.
(f∘g)(x) means f(g(x)). Do g first, then feed its answer into f. The order matters.
An inverse undoes a function. If f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. To find it, swap input and output and solve.
y = a·f(x − h) + k. h slides right, k slides up, a stretches (and flips if negative). Do stretches first, then shifts.
Even: f(−x) = f(x), the graph is mirror-symmetric about the y-axis. Odd: f(−x) = −f(x), it looks the same after a half-turn about the origin.
x² is even, x³ is odd
qd2: A square with side s has area s². Going backwards, √(s²) = s. Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.
If two numbers multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. So (x − p)(x − q) = 0 means x = p or x = q.
y = a(x − h)² + k has its turning point at (h, k). It opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0.
For ax² + bx + c = 0, x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. It always works.
D = b² − 4ac tells how many real roots: D > 0 two, D = 0 one, D < 0 none (two complex roots).
Define i so that i² = −1. A complex number is a + bi. Add and multiply like algebra, then replace i² with −1.
The powers of i repeat every 4: i, −1, −i, 1. To find iⁿ, divide n by 4 and use the remainder.
For ax² + bx + c = 0 the roots add to −b/a and multiply to c/a, even when they are complex.
pl: x³ means x · x · x. A term is a number times powers of x. A polynomial is a sum of terms. Its degree is the highest power.
Combine like terms to add. To multiply, give every term in the first factor a turn with every term in the second.
When you divide f(x) by (x − a), the remainder is f(a). So plugging in a number is a shortcut for division.
(x − a) is a factor of f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0. Roots and factors are the same information.
A polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots, counting repeats and complex roots. Odd degree always crosses the x-axis at least once.
Far out, only the highest-degree term matters. Even degree: both ends go the same way. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways. A negative leading coefficient flips the picture.
A rational root p/q (lowest terms) of an integer polynomial has p dividing the constant term and q dividing the leading coefficient.
For x³ + bx² + cx + d the roots add to −b, pair-products add to c and all three multiply to −d.
roots r, s, t: r + s + t = −b
ra: A fraction a/b means a ÷ b. You can simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the same number, like 12/18 = 2/3.
A rational expression is a polynomial divided by a polynomial. Simplify by factoring and cancelling common factors, never by cancelling terms that are added.
The denominator can never be 0. Every x that makes it 0 is left out of the domain.
If a factor cancels, the graph has a hole. If a factor in the denominator stays, the graph shoots off to infinity there: a vertical asymptote.
Compare degrees. Top lower: y = 0. Same degree: y = (leading coefficient of top) ÷ (leading coefficient of bottom). Top higher: no horizontal asymptote.
Multiply both sides by the common denominator to clear the fractions. Then check each answer, because a solution that makes a denominator 0 is extraneous.
Direct: y = kx, both grow together. Inverse: y = k/x, one grows as the other shrinks. More workers means fewer days.
3 workers take 12 days → 6 workers take 6 days
Rates add. If A does a job in a hours and B in b hours, together they finish in ab/(a + b) hours.
ex: 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. The small raised number counts how many times the base is used.
If a plant doubles every day, after n days it is 2ⁿ times bigger. This kind of growth starts slowly and then explodes.
y = a·bˣ. a is the starting amount and b is the growth factor. If b > 1 it grows. If 0 < b < 1 it decays.
b⁰ = 1 and b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. A negative exponent means flip, not negative.
Growing 8% a year multiplies by 1.08. Losing 20% multiplies by 0.80.
With n compounds a year: A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ. More compounds give slightly more money.
After one half-life, half remains. After two, a quarter. Amount = start × (½)^(time ÷ half-life).
If the bases match, set the exponents equal. Otherwise take a logarithm of both sides.
lg: log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.
log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.
log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b. Logs turn multiplying into adding.
log(aⁿ) = n·log a. This is how logs pull exponents down so you can solve for them.
log_b x = log x / log b. It lets a calculator find any log.
Combine logs into one, rewrite as an exponent, solve, then check that every log's input is positive.
ln is the log with base e ≈ 2.718. ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
sq: A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.
You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.
Adding the terms: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Gauss found 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 5050 by pairing ends.
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Each term is r times the last.
If |r| < 1 the terms shrink and the total settles on S = a₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 it never settles.
Σ means add. Σ from k = 1 to 4 of 2k means 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Recursive: each term from the one before (aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3). Explicit: each term from its position (aₙ = 3n + 1).
tc: A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
The sides of a right triangle
In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.
To find a side, write the ratio that has it and solve. To find an angle, use the inverse button: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.
One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. A half-turn is π radians, so 180° = π rad.
On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). So cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.
30°, 45° and 60° have exact values: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine reads the same list backwards.
Any angle has a reference angle (the acute angle to the x-axis). Find its value, then use the quadrant to choose + or −: All Students Take Calculus (all, sine, tangent, cosine).
tg: Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.
The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.
The period is the length of one full wave. For y = sin(bx), the period is 360°/b (or 2π/b in radians). A bigger b squeezes the wave.
In y = sin(x − c) the wave slides right by c. A minus sign inside means right, plus means left.
In y = sin x + d the whole wave moves up by d. The midline is y = d. Maximum = d + |a| and minimum = d − |a|.
y = 2 sin x + 1: ranges from −1 to 3
Cosine is sine shifted left by 90°. Tangent repeats every 180° and has vertical asymptotes where cosine is 0.
To model a wave: find the midline (average of max and min), the amplitude (half the difference), and the period. Then choose sine or cosine and a shift.
ti: An identity is an equation that is true for every allowed angle, like a rule of arithmetic that always works.
On the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Knowing one of them gives you the other.
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. That is why tangent has an asymptote wherever cosine is 0.
sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ.
sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.
Isolate the trig function, find the reference angle, use the quadrants to list all answers in the interval, then check.
Because trig functions repeat, equations have many solutions. In [0°, 360°) sin x = ½ has two: 30° and 150°.
sin⁻¹ gives one answer in a restricted range (−90° to 90°). The equation sin x = k can have a second answer you must add yourself.
tl: Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.
c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.
Given two sides and an angle not between them, there may be 0, 1 or 2 triangles. Check whether the side opposite the angle can reach the base.
Area = ½ab sin C. It works for any two sides and the angle between them.
A vector has a size (magnitude) and a direction. Write it as components (x, y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²).
Add components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d). A plane's ground velocity is its air velocity plus the wind's.
a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ = |a||b| cos θ. If the dot product is 0 the vectors are perpendicular.
cn: The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.
A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).
An ellipse is a stretched circle: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. The two foci are c units from the center where c² = a² − b² (a is the longer half-axis).
A hyperbola has two branches: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. The foci satisfy c² = a² + b² and the asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x.
e = c/a measures how stretched a conic is. Circle e = 0, ellipse 0 < e < 1, parabola e = 1, hyperbola e > 1.
Look at the squared terms. Same sign and same coefficient: circle. Same sign, different coefficients: ellipse. Opposite signs: hyperbola. Only one squared variable: parabola.
Planets move in ellipses, satellite dishes are parabolas, and whispering galleries use ellipses to carry sound between the foci.
pp: Two ways to name a point
Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.
x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).
r = 2 is a circle. r = θ spirals outward. Roses, cardioids and limaçons come from r = a cos(nθ) and similar rules.
Write x and y as functions of a third variable t, like time. They describe motion along a path.
Solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get a relation between x and y.
Plot a + bi at (a, b). Its modulus is √(a² + b²) and its argument is the angle from the real axis.
In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the angles. So (r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis(nθ).
lm: Look at 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … The numbers never reach 1 but get as close as you like. We say they approach 1.
lim f(x) = L as x → a means f(x) gets as close to L as you want when x is close enough to a. The value at a itself does not matter.
For polynomials and most everyday functions, just plug the number in.
If substitution gives 0/0, factor and cancel the common piece, then substitute.
The left limit looks from below, the right limit from above. The limit exists only if both agree.
As x grows huge, only the highest powers matter. Compare the leading terms.
A function is continuous at a if the limit equals the value: no jumps, holes or breaks. You can draw it without lifting your pencil.
lim sin x / x = 1 when x is in radians. This is the key to the derivative of sine.
dv: Speed is how fast distance changes. The derivative is a rate of change at one instant, like a speedometer reading.
The derivative f′(x) is the slope of the tangent line at x. It is the limit of the slope between two points as they come together.
d/dx of xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹. Constants disappear and constants multiplying stay.
Take the derivative of each term separately.
(uv)′ = u′v + uv′. The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives.
For a function inside a function, take the derivative of the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
(sin x)′ = cos x, (cos x)′ = −sin x, (eˣ)′ = eˣ, (ln x)′ = 1/x.
da: If s(t) is position, velocity is s′(t) and acceleration is s″(t).
If f′ > 0 the function rises. If f′ < 0 it falls. Where f′ = 0 there may be a peak or valley.
Solve f′(x) = 0 to find candidates for maximum and minimum points.
At a critical point, f″ > 0 means a valley (minimum) and f″ < 0 means a peak (maximum).
f″ > 0: the curve bends upward like a cup. f″ < 0: it bends downward like a cap.
Write what you want to maximize or minimize as a function of one variable, take the derivative, set it to 0 and check the endpoints.
When two quantities are linked, their rates are linked too. Differentiate the relationship with respect to time.
Near x = a, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). The tangent line is a good estimate close by.
in: Area is how much space is inside a shape. We can estimate the area under a curve by adding up thin rectangles.
Split the interval into slices, make a rectangle for each, and add the areas. More slices give a better estimate.
∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the exact signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Area below the axis counts as negative.
An antiderivative of f is a function whose derivative is f. For powers: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.
∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f. Derivatives and integrals undo each other.
Average value = (1/(b − a)) ∫ f. Integrating a rate gives total change, like integrating speed to get distance.
For ∫f(g(x))g′(x) dx, let u = g(x). The messy part becomes a simple integral in u.
Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve and integrate across the interval.
iv: An inverse function undoes another: if f turns x into y, then f⁻¹ turns y back into x. Check: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Note f⁻¹(x) is NOT 1/f(x).
Trig takes an angle, inverse takes a ratio
sin, cos and tan turn an angle into a ratio. sin⁻¹ (also written arcsin), cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ turn a ratio back into an angle. That is how you find a missing angle in a right triangle.
Sine repeats forever, so many angles share one ratio. To make an inverse, we keep one piece: arcsin gives −90° to 90°, arccos gives 0° to 180°, arctan gives −90° to 90° (open).
Check degree or radian mode first. Use the sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ keys. arcsin and arccos only accept inputs from −1 to 1; arctan accepts any number.
id: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B. cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B. Notice the sign flips for cosine.
Put B = A in the sum formulas: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A and cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 1 − 2 sin²A = 2 cos²A − 1.
Solve the cosine double-angle formula for the half angle: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2. Pick the sign from the quadrant.
Adding the sum and difference formulas gives 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B). The same idea turns products into sums and sums into products.

glossary: A rule that gives each input exactly one output.
A function that undoes another: swaps inputs and outputs.
b² − 4ac; tells how many real roots a quadratic has.
A sum of terms that are numbers times whole-number powers of x.
An input where the function equals 0.
Dividing f(x) by (x − a) leaves remainder f(a).
(x − a) is a factor of f exactly when f(a) = 0.
stuck: Write what you know and what you must find.
Try a small number first to see the pattern.
Sketch a graph. What shape is it?
Check your answer by plugging it back in.

lessons.title: Input and output · Function notation

cards.t: A function is a rule that turns every input into exactly one output, like a vending machine: press B4 and you always get the same snack.

lab.hook: A function is a machine: put a number in, one number comes out.
lab.note: Put in {x}, the machine gives {=2*x+1|0}. The same input always gives the same output.

pre.q: If the rule is "double it, then add 1", what comes out when 3 goes in?

lab.take: A function gives exactly one output for each input.

cards.t: f(x) is read “f of x”. It means: use the rule f on the number x. To find f(4), put 4 into the rule.

lab.hook: f(x) is just a name for the output.
lab.note: f({x}) means: replace every x with {x}. So f({x}) = {x}² − 3 = {=x^2-3|0}.
lab.take: f(2) is read "f of 2". It does not mean f times 2.

cards.h: Tables, graphs and the vertical line test
cards.t: A graph shows a function if no vertical line touches it twice. If one input had two outputs, the machine would be broken.

lab.hook: A graph is a picture of every input-output pair. Slide a and watch the picture.
lab.out: Each x has one y: y = {a}·x. Every vertical line crosses this graph once.
lab.take: Vertical line test: if any vertical line hits a graph twice, it is not a function.

lessons.title: Domain and range · Composing functions

cards.t: The domain is every input that is allowed. The range is every output you can get. You cannot divide by zero, and you cannot take the square root of a negative number in the real numbers.

lab.hook: Domain = inputs allowed. Range = outputs you get. Slide c to shift the square-root curve.
lab.out: sqrt(x − {c}) only works when x ≥ {c}. The outputs are 0 and up.

pre.q: Can you take the square root of −4 and get a real number?
pre.why: No real number times itself is negative, so inputs below the start are not allowed.

lab.take: Domain: allowed x-values. Range: possible y-values.

cards.t: (f∘g)(x) means f(g(x)). Do g first, then feed its answer into f. The order matters.

lab.hook: Feed one machine into another: f(g(x)).
lab.take: Work from the inside out: do g first, then f.

cards.t: An inverse undoes a function. If f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. To find it, swap input and output and solve.

lab.hook: An inverse undoes the function. Its graph is the mirror image across the line y = x.
lab.out: f(x) = {a}x + 1 and its inverse (x − 1)/{a} are mirror images across the diagonal.
lab.take: f⁻¹ swaps inputs and outputs. It is not 1/f.

lessons.title: Transformations · Even and odd functions

cards.t: y = a·f(x − h) + k. h slides right, k slides up, a stretches (and flips if negative). Do stretches first, then shifts.

lab.hook: Move and stretch the parabola y = a(x − h)² + k.
lab.out: Vertex at ({h}, {k}). Gold = original y = x².

pre.q: Which way does y = (x − 2)² move y = x²?
pre.why: The graph shifts the opposite way from the sign inside the bracket: right 2.

lab.take: (x − h) moves right by h. + k moves up by k. a stretches or flips.

cards.t: Even: f(−x) = f(x), the graph is mirror-symmetric about the y-axis. Odd: f(−x) = −f(x), it looks the same after a half-turn about the origin.
cards.f: x² is even, x³ is odd

lab.hook: Even functions are mirror images across the y-axis. Odd ones spin 180° about the origin.
lab.out: x^{n}: n is {n}. Even n gives a mirror graph. Odd n gives a spin.

lessons.title: Squares and square roots · Solving by factoring

cards.t: A square with side s has area s². Going backwards, √(s²) = s. Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.

lab.hook: A square root asks: what number times itself gives this?
lab.note: A square with side {s} has area {=s^2|0}. Going backwards: √{=s^2|0} = {s}.

cards.t: If two numbers multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. So (x − p)(x − q) = 0 means x = p or x = q.

lab.hook: The roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis. y = (x − p)(x − q).
lab.out: Crosses the axis at x = {p} and x = {q}.
lab.take: Zero-product rule: if (x − p)(x − q) = 0, then x = p or x = q.

cards.t: y = a(x − h)² + k has its turning point at (h, k). It opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0.

lab.hook: Vertex form shows the turning point right away.
lab.out: The vertex is ({h}, {k}). Positive a opens up, negative a opens down.

lessons.title: The quadratic formula · The discriminant

cards.t: For ax² + bx + c = 0, x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. It always works.

lab.hook: Change a, b, c and see where the parabola meets the x-axis.

cards.t: D = b² − 4ac tells how many real roots: D > 0 two, D = 0 one, D < 0 none (two complex roots).

lab.hook: The discriminant b² − 4ac tells how many times the curve touches the x-axis.
lab.out: Discriminant = {=b^2-4*c}. Positive: 2 crossings. Zero: touches once. Negative: none.

pre.q: If a parabola floats above the x-axis, how many real roots does it have?
pre.why: It never touches the axis, so no real roots.

cards.t: Define i so that i² = −1. A complex number is a + bi. Add and multiply like algebra, then replace i² with −1.

lessons.title: Powers of i · Roots and coefficients (Vieta)

cards.t: The powers of i repeat every 4: i, −1, −i, 1. To find iⁿ, divide n by 4 and use the remainder.
For ax² + bx + c = 0 the roots add to −b/a and multiply to c/a, even when they are complex.

lessons.title: Powers and terms · Adding and multiplying polynomials

cards.t: x³ means x · x · x. A term is a number times powers of x. A polynomial is a sum of terms. Its degree is the highest power.

lab.hook: A polynomial is a sum of terms like a·xⁿ.

cards.t: Combine like terms to add. To multiply, give every term in the first factor a turn with every term in the second.
When you divide f(x) by (x − a), the remainder is f(a). So plugging in a number is a shortcut for division.

lab.hook: Dividing by (x − a) leaves the remainder p(a).
lab.out: p({a}) = {=a^3-2*a^2-a+2|0}. That is the remainder when you divide by (x − {a}).

lessons.title: The factor theorem · How many roots?

cards.t: (x − a) is a factor of f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0. Roots and factors are the same information.

lab.hook: If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor. Slide a until the point lands on the axis.
lab.out: p({a}) = {=a^3-2*a^2-a+2|0}. Zero means (x − {a}) divides it exactly.

cards.t: A polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots, counting repeats and complex roots. Odd degree always crosses the x-axis at least once.
Far out, only the highest-degree term matters. Even degree: both ends go the same way. Odd degree: the ends go opposite ways. A negative leading coefficient flips the picture.

lab.hook: Far left and far right, only the highest power matters.
lab.out: Degree {n}, coefficient {a}.
lab.take: Even degree: both ends go the same way. Odd degree: ends go opposite ways.

lessons.title: Rational root theorem · Vieta for cubics

cards.t: A rational root p/q (lowest terms) of an integer polynomial has p dividing the constant term and q dividing the leading coefficient.
For x³ + bx² + cx + d the roots add to −b, pair-products add to c and all three multiply to −d.
cards.f: roots r, s, t: r + s + t = −b

lessons.title: Fractions are division · Rational expressions

cards.t: A fraction a/b means a ÷ b. You can simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the same number, like 12/18 = 2/3.

lab.hook: A fraction is a division. Watch what happens as the bottom gets small.
lab.note: 1 ÷ {d} = {=1/d|3}. A smaller bottom makes a bigger answer.

cards.t: A rational expression is a polynomial divided by a polynomial. Simplify by factoring and cancelling common factors, never by cancelling terms that are added.
The denominator can never be 0. Every x that makes it 0 is left out of the domain.

lessons.title: Vertical asymptotes and holes · Horizontal asymptotes

cards.t: If a factor cancels, the graph has a hole. If a factor in the denominator stays, the graph shoots off to infinity there: a vertical asymptote.

lab.hook: Dividing by something near 0 blows up. Slide a to move the asymptote.
lab.out: The bottom is zero at x = {a}, so the graph shoots off there.
lab.take: A vertical asymptote sits where the denominator is 0 and the numerator is not.

cards.t: Compare degrees. Top lower: y = 0. Same degree: y = (leading coefficient of top) ÷ (leading coefficient of bottom). Top higher: no horizontal asymptote.

lab.hook: Far from zero, y = (x + 1)/(x − 1) settles near 1.
lab.out: As x gets huge, y gets close to 1.

cards.t: Multiply both sides by the common denominator to clear the fractions. Then check each answer, because a solution that makes a denominator 0 is extraneous.

lessons.title: Direct and inverse variation · Work and rate problems

cards.t: Direct: y = kx, both grow together. Inverse: y = k/x, one grows as the other shrinks. More workers means fewer days.
cards.f: 3 workers take 12 days → 6 workers take 6 days

lab.hook: Direct: y = kx grows together. Inverse: y = k/x trades off.
lab.out: Blue: y = {k}x. Gold: y = {k}/x.

cards.t: Rates add. If A does a job in a hours and B in b hours, together they finish in ab/(a + b) hours.

lessons.title: Repeated multiplication · Doubling and tripling

cards.t: 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. The small raised number counts how many times the base is used.
If a plant doubles every day, after n days it is 2ⁿ times bigger. This kind of growth starts slowly and then explodes.

lab.hook: Doubling over and over becomes huge very fast.
lab.eq: Start at 1 and double n times

pre.q: A coin doubles in value 10 times starting at 1 cent. About how much?

cards.t: y = a·bˣ. a is the starting amount and b is the growth factor. If b > 1 it grows. If 0 < b < 1 it decays.

lab.hook: y = a·bˣ. Change the growth factor b.
lab.out: b = {b}. Above 1 the curve grows; below 1 it shrinks.
lab.take: b > 1 is growth. 0 < b < 1 is decay.

lessons.title: Negative and zero exponents · Percent growth and decay

cards.t: b⁰ = 1 and b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. A negative exponent means flip, not negative.
Growing 8% a year multiplies by 1.08. Losing 20% multiplies by 0.80.

lab.hook: A 5% rise multiplies by 1.05 each time.

cards.t: With n compounds a year: A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ. More compounds give slightly more money.

lessons.title: Half-life · Solving exponential equations

cards.t: After one half-life, half remains. After two, a quarter. Amount = start × (½)^(time ÷ half-life).

lab.hook: After each half-life, half is left.
lab.out: Half-life = {h}. After {h} steps there is 50%; after {=2*h|0}, 25%.

cards.t: If the bases match, set the exponents equal. Otherwise take a logarithm of both sides.

lessons.title: What a logarithm asks · Common logs

cards.t: log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.

lab.hook: A log asks: what power do I need?

cards.t: log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.

lessons.title: Product and quotient rules · Power rule

cards.t: log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b. Logs turn multiplying into adding.

lab.hook: Logs turn multiplying into adding.
lab.note: If A = 10^{a} and B = 10^{b}, then A×B = 10^{=a+b|0}. Multiply → add the exponents.

cards.t: log(aⁿ) = n·log a. This is how logs pull exponents down so you can solve for them.
log_b x = log x / log b. It lets a calculator find any log.

lessons.title: Solving log equations · Natural log

cards.t: Combine logs into one, rewrite as an exponent, solve, then check that every log's input is positive.
ln is the log with base e ≈ 2.718. ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x.

lessons.title: Patterns and sequences · Arithmetic sequences

cards.t: A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.

lab.hook: A sequence is a list that follows a rule.

cards.t: You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.

lab.hook: Each term adds the same amount d.

cards.t: You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.

lab.hook: Each term multiplies by the same ratio r.

lessons.title: Arithmetic series · Geometric series

cards.t: Adding the terms: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Gauss found 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 5050 by pairing ends.
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Each term is r times the last.
If |r| < 1 the terms shrink and the total settles on S = a₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 it never settles.

lessons.title: Sigma notation · Recursive and explicit rules

cards.t: Σ means add. Σ from k = 1 to 4 of 2k means 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Recursive: each term from the one before (aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3). Explicit: each term from its position (aₙ = 3n + 1).

lessons.title: Turns and degrees · The sides of a right triangle

cards.t: A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.

cards.h: The sides of a right triangle
cards.t: In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.

lab.hook: Slide the angle and the size. Watch the ratios.
lab.take: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. The ratios depend only on the angle.

lessons.title: Finding sides and angles · Radians

cards.t: To find a side, write the ratio that has it and solve. To find an angle, use the inverse button: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.
One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. A half-turn is π radians, so 180° = π rad.

lab.hook: A radian is an angle measured by arc length.
lab.note: {d}° = {=d*pi/180|3} radians. A half turn (180°) is π ≈ 3.14.

cards.t: On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). So cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.

lab.hook: Drag the angle around the circle. Read sin and cos from the point.

pre.q: At 90°, the point is straight up. What is cos 90°?
pre.why: The point is (0, 1): x = cos = 0, y = sin = 1.

lab.take: On the unit circle, the point is (cos θ, sin θ).

lessons.title: Special angles · Reference angles and signs

cards.t: 30°, 45° and 60° have exact values: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine reads the same list backwards.

lab.hook: Set the angle to 30°, 45°, 60°. Notice the values.

cards.t: Any angle has a reference angle (the acute angle to the x-axis). Find its value, then use the quadrant to choose + or −: All Students Take Calculus (all, sine, tangent, cosine).

lab.hook: Move through the four quadrants. When are sin and cos negative?

pre.q: In quadrant II (90°–180°), which is negative?
pre.why: x is negative there, so cos is negative while sin stays positive.

lessons.title: Waves in everyday life · The sine graph

cards.t: Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.

lab.hook: Trace the unit circle height as the angle grows.
lab.out: One full wave every 360°.

cards.t: The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.

lab.hook: Amplitude is how tall the wave is from the middle.
lab.out: Amplitude = {A}: the wave goes up to {A} and down to −{A}.

lessons.title: Period · Phase shift

cards.t: The period is the length of one full wave. For y = sin(bx), the period is 360°/b (or 2π/b in radians). A bigger b squeezes the wave.

lab.hook: Period is how long one full wave takes.

cards.t: In y = sin(x − c) the wave slides right by c. A minus sign inside means right, plus means left.

lab.hook: Phase shift slides the wave left or right.
lab.out: Blue is shifted right by {c}°. Gold is the original.

cards.t: In y = sin x + d the whole wave moves up by d. The midline is y = d. Maximum = d + |a| and minimum = d − |a|.
cards.f: y = 2 sin x + 1: ranges from −1 to 3

lab.hook: Vertical shift moves the middle line up or down.
lab.out: Middle line at y = {k}.

lessons.title: Cosine and tangent graphs · Modeling with sinusoids

cards.t: Cosine is sine shifted left by 90°. Tangent repeats every 180° and has vertical asymptotes where cosine is 0.

lab.hook: Cosine is sine shifted. Tangent has asymptotes.
lab.out: Cosine (blue) is sine (gold) shifted 90° left.

cards.t: To model a wave: find the midline (average of max and min), the amplitude (half the difference), and the period. Then choose sine or cosine and a shift.

lab.hook: A Ferris wheel height is a wave: height = r·sin + middle.
lab.out: One turn every {T} minutes. Height swings from 1 m to 15 m.

lessons.title: Same value, different look · The Pythagorean identity

cards.t: An identity is an equation that is true for every allowed angle, like a rule of arithmetic that always works.

lab.hook: Two different-looking expressions can always agree. Test it.

cards.t: On the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Knowing one of them gives you the other.

lab.hook: The point sits on a circle of radius 1, so x² + y² = 1.

cards.t: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. That is why tangent has an asymptote wherever cosine is 0.

lessons.title: Double-angle identities · Sum and difference identities

cards.t: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ.
sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.
Isolate the trig function, find the reference angle, use the quadrants to list all answers in the interval, then check.

lessons.title: Many solutions · Inverse trig functions

cards.t: Because trig functions repeat, equations have many solutions. In [0°, 360°) sin x = ½ has two: 30° and 150°.
sin⁻¹ gives one answer in a restricted range (−90° to 90°). The equation sin x = k can have a second answer you must add yourself.

lessons.title: Undoing a function · Trig takes an angle, inverse takes a ratio

cards.t: An inverse function undoes another: if f turns x into y, then f⁻¹ turns y back into x. Check: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Note f⁻¹(x) is NOT 1/f(x).

cards.h: Trig takes an angle, inverse takes a ratio
cards.t: sin, cos and tan turn an angle into a ratio. sin⁻¹ (also written arcsin), cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ turn a ratio back into an angle. That is how you find a missing angle in a right triangle.

lab.hook: Inverse sine turns a ratio back into an angle.

pre.why: The inverse gives the angle back: 30°.

cards.t: Sine repeats forever, so many angles share one ratio. To make an inverse, we keep one piece: arcsin gives −90° to 90°, arccos gives 0° to 180°, arctan gives −90° to 90° (open).
Check degree or radian mode first. Use the sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ keys. arcsin and arccos only accept inputs from −1 to 1; arctan accepts any number.

lessons.title: Sum and difference · Double angles

cards.t: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B. cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B. Notice the sign flips for cosine.

lab.hook: Check sin(A + B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB.

cards.t: Put B = A in the sum formulas: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A and cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 1 − 2 sin²A = 2 cos²A − 1.

lab.hook: sin 2θ and 2 sin θ cos θ are the same.

cards.t: Solve the cosine double-angle formula for the half angle: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2. Pick the sign from the quadrant.
Adding the sum and difference formulas gives 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B). The same idea turns products into sums and sums into products.

lessons.title: Triangles that are not right · Law of Sines

cards.t: Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.

lab.hook: In every triangle, side ÷ sin(opposite angle) is the same.
lab.eq: a / sin A = b / sin B

cards.t: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.

lessons.title: The ambiguous case (SSA) · Area with sine

cards.t: Given two sides and an angle not between them, there may be 0, 1 or 2 triangles. Check whether the side opposite the angle can reach the base.
Area = ½ab sin C. It works for any two sides and the angle between them.
A vector has a size (magnitude) and a direction. Write it as components (x, y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²).

lessons.title: Adding vectors · Dot product and angles

cards.t: Add components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d). A plane's ground velocity is its air velocity plus the wind's.
a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ = |a||b| cos θ. If the dot product is 0 the vectors are perpendicular.

lessons.title: Distance and midpoint · Circles

cards.t: The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.
A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

lab.hook: A circle is every point at the same distance r from the center.

cards.t: A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).

lab.hook: A parabola opens toward its focus.
lab.out: y = x²/(4·{p}). The focus is {p} above the vertex.

lessons.title: Ellipses · Hyperbolas

cards.t: An ellipse is a stretched circle: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. The two foci are c units from the center where c² = a² − b² (a is the longer half-axis).
A hyperbola has two branches: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. The foci satisfy c² = a² + b² and the asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x.
e = c/a measures how stretched a conic is. Circle e = 0, ellipse 0 < e < 1, parabola e = 1, hyperbola e > 1.

lessons.title: Identifying a conic · Real-world conics

cards.t: Look at the squared terms. Same sign and same coefficient: circle. Same sign, different coefficients: ellipse. Opposite signs: hyperbola. Only one squared variable: parabola.
Planets move in ellipses, satellite dishes are parabolas, and whispering galleries use ellipses to carry sound between the foci.

lessons.title: Two ways to name a point · Converting polar to rectangular

cards.h: Two ways to name a point
cards.t: Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.

lab.hook: (r, θ): how far and which direction.

cards.t: x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).

lessons.title: Polar curves · Parametric equations

cards.t: r = 2 is a circle. r = θ spirals outward. Roses, cardioids and limaçons come from r = a cos(nθ) and similar rules.
Write x and y as functions of a third variable t, like time. They describe motion along a path.
Solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get a relation between x and y.

lessons.title: The complex plane · De Moivre's theorem

cards.t: Plot a + bi at (a, b). Its modulus is √(a² + b²) and its argument is the angle from the real axis.
In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the angles. So (r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis(nθ).

lessons.title: Getting closer and closer · What a limit means

cards.t: Look at 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … The numbers never reach 1 but get as close as you like. We say they approach 1.

lab.hook: A limit asks what y does as x creeps toward a number.
lab.out: As x gets near 1, y gets near 2, even though x = 1 is not allowed.

cards.t: lim f(x) = L as x → a means f(x) gets as close to L as you want when x is close enough to a. The value at a itself does not matter.
For polynomials and most everyday functions, just plug the number in.

lessons.title: 0/0: factor and cancel · One-sided limits

cards.t: If substitution gives 0/0, factor and cancel the common piece, then substitute.
The left limit looks from below, the right limit from above. The limit exists only if both agree.
As x grows huge, only the highest powers matter. Compare the leading terms.

lessons.title: Continuity · Famous limits

cards.t: A function is continuous at a if the limit equals the value: no jumps, holes or breaks. You can draw it without lifting your pencil.
lim sin x / x = 1 when x is in radians. This is the key to the derivative of sine.

lessons.title: Rate of change · Slope of a curve

cards.t: Speed is how fast distance changes. The derivative is a rate of change at one instant, like a speedometer reading.
The derivative f′(x) is the slope of the tangent line at x. It is the limit of the slope between two points as they come together.

lab.hook: The derivative is the slope of the tangent line.
lab.out: At x = {a}, the slope of x² is {=2*a|1}.

cards.t: d/dx of xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹. Constants disappear and constants multiplying stay.

lab.hook: Power rule: the derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹.

lessons.title: Sums and differences · Product rule

cards.t: Take the derivative of each term separately.
(uv)′ = u′v + uv′. The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives.
(u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v².

lessons.title: Chain rule · Trig, exponential and log derivatives

cards.t: For a function inside a function, take the derivative of the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
(sin x)′ = cos x, (cos x)′ = −sin x, (eˣ)′ = eˣ, (ln x)′ = 1/x.

lessons.title: Position, velocity, acceleration · Increasing and decreasing

cards.t: If s(t) is position, velocity is s′(t) and acceleration is s″(t).
If f′ > 0 the function rises. If f′ < 0 it falls. Where f′ = 0 there may be a peak or valley.
Solve f′(x) = 0 to find candidates for maximum and minimum points.

lab.hook: The curve flattens at maximum and minimum points.
lab.out: Slope at x = {a}: {=3*a^2-3|1}. It is 0 at x = ±1.

lessons.title: The second derivative test · Concavity

cards.t: At a critical point, f″ > 0 means a valley (minimum) and f″ < 0 means a peak (maximum).
f″ > 0: the curve bends upward like a cup. f″ < 0: it bends downward like a cap.
Write what you want to maximize or minimize as a function of one variable, take the derivative, set it to 0 and check the endpoints.

lessons.title: Related rates · Linear approximation

cards.t: When two quantities are linked, their rates are linked too. Differentiate the relationship with respect to time.
Near x = a, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). The tangent line is a good estimate close by.

lessons.title: Area by counting · Riemann sums

cards.t: Area is how much space is inside a shape. We can estimate the area under a curve by adding up thin rectangles.
Split the interval into slices, make a rectangle for each, and add the areas. More slices give a better estimate.
∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the exact signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Area below the axis counts as negative.

lessons.title: Antiderivatives · Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

cards.t: An antiderivative of f is a function whose derivative is f. For powers: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.
∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f. Derivatives and integrals undo each other.
Average value = (1/(b − a)) ∫ f. Integrating a rate gives total change, like integrating speed to get distance.

lessons.title: Substitution · Area between curves

cards.t: For ∫f(g(x))g′(x) dx, let u = g(x). The messy part becomes a simple integral in u.
Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve and integrate across the interval.
